title: High Throughput Single-cell and Multiple-cell Micro-encapsulation
protocol: Design a micro-channel pattern as shown in Figure 1 using AutoCAD.
Employ a third party manufacturer to print a high resolution transparency mask on Mylar film or quartz.
Channels should be transparent on a dark background.
Create a silicon and SU-8 photoresist master for replica molding.
Spin SU-8 2050 negative photoresist on a clean silicon wafer using a spin-coater at manufacturer's recommended rpm to create a 52 μm thick layer.
Soft bake the spun SU-8 layer as per standard procedure.
Remove edge bead from the baked SU-8 layer.
UV expose the SU-8 layer through a contact mask.
Post-exposure bake the UV exposed layer according to manufacturer guidelines.
Develop the post-baked layer using SU-8 developer solution.
Measure the actual thickness of the developed SU-8 layer using a Dektak profilometer.
Tape the master mold onto the bottom of a Petri dish for PDMS replica molding.
Mix 20 g of PDMS elastomer base with 2 g of curing agent in a 10:1 ratio w/w.
Pour well-mixed PDMS precursor onto the silicon master to create a 2-3 mm final thickness layer.
Place the master mold and PDMS in a vacuum desiccator.
Slowly decrease chamber pressure from 0" Hg to -27" Hg over 20 minutes to avoid excessive foaming.
Leave device in vacuum chamber at -27" Hg for 30 minutes or until air bubbles disappear.
Release vacuum and move master mold and PDMS to a 65 °C oven.
Cure the PDMS in the oven for a minimum of four hours.
Remove the device from the oven.
Allow the device to cool.
Carefully cut around the circular wafer with a precision knife.
Peel out the PDMS from the wafer.
Cut out the device outline as shown in Figure 1 with a scalpel.
Punch fluidic ports (three per device) in the three round regions shown in Figure 1 using a biopsy punch.
Use a 0.75 mm outer diameter punch for this procedure.
Adhere scotch tape to the patterned side of the PDMS.
Peel off the tape to remove dust from the PDMS surface.
Plasma treat the patterned side of the PDMS and a clean 3" x 1" glass microscope slide using a hand-held laboratory corona treater.
Wave the electrode about 1/4" above each surface for around 20 seconds.
Immediately bring the treated surfaces into contact to form a strong permanent bond.
Place the device on a metal plate.
Place the metal plate in a cool oven and set the oven to 120 °C.
Bake overnight to complete bonding and return the PDMS to its original hydrophobic state.
Alternatively, inject Aquapel into the fluidic ports using a 1 mL syringe and a syringe needle.
Purge air into the fluidic ports without breaking the PDMS to glass bond.
Aggressively repeat the air purge on all inlet ports while wiping off any excess Aquapel.
Aggressively repeat the air purge on all outlet ports while wiping off any excess Aquapel.
Prepare a cell culture according to established procedures for your chosen cell type.
Adjust particle size to 8-15 μm for encapsulation in the device.
Use 9.9 μm polystyrene microspheres as cell surrogates for method demonstration.
Gently mix to prepare an aqueous particle or cell suspension.
Calculate desired cell or particle concentration based on ordered train spacing and channel size.
Centrifuge stock sample if necessary, remove supernatant liquid, and re-suspend particles by gentle mixing.
Prepare an adequate volume of suspension considering the collection volume and flow tuning time.
Power on the inverted optical microscope and high speed camera.
Focus and inspect the channels for clogs and debris by moving the device or using a motorized microscope stage.
Remove small debris when liquid flows through the channels.
Select another channel if large debris or obvious clogs are present.
Cut three lengths of PVC tubing for the aqueous inlet, oil inlet, and emulsion outlet.
Cut tubing ends at a 45° angle to facilitate insertion into fluidic ports.
Press fit the tube ends into the fluidic ports punched in Step 1 using tweezers.
Press fit two 30 gauge blunt-tip stainless steel syringe needles into the free ends of the respective aqueous and oil inlet tubes.
Place the outlet tubing into a waste reservoir.
Move the device and attached tubing to the microscope stage.
Align and focus on the device nozzle using an available objective (20x was used for this experiment).
Adjust for Köhler illumination and other microscope settings as required for optimal recording.
Fill a 1 mL syringe with the well-mixed aqueous phase.
Fill a 3 mL syringe with the oil phase solution prepared in Step 2.
Tilt one syringe vertically and flick to move air bubbles to the syringe outlet.
Slowly depress plunger enough to push the air to the syringe tip.
Hold the syringe vertically, connect the syringes to the respective syringe needle already attached to the device.
Depress plunger to force the air through the syringe needle dead volume until fluid is pushed through the tubing almost to the device.
Securely mount the 1 mL syringe to a syringe pump and engage the plunger block.
Repeat connections for the second syringe and mount to a second syringe pump.
Power on each syringe pump and program using the pump manufacturer's protocols.
Set the initial flow rates to Qoil = 50 μL/min and Qaq = 5 μL/min for the oil phase and aqueous phase, respectively.
Start the pumps.
Wait for each fluid to enter the device and fill the channels, pushing out remaining dead air.
Temporarily increase flow rates if there is a large amount of air in the inlet tubing.
Observe the formation of drops at the nozzle using initial flow rates.
Reduce camera field of view to only the nozzle to maximize frame rate and reduce memory requirements.
Capture sample videos and confirm that the sampling rate is adequate to avoid aliasing.
Start with low aqueous flow rates to avoid jetting.
Slowly increase the aqueous flow rate to observe ordering of particles in the long aqueous solution channel as the flow rate increases.
Physically tilt the syringe pump toward the syringe outlet if particle concentration is too low and sample was not buoyancy matched.
Periodically rotate the syringe along its axis to reduce undesired settling.
Adjust the oil flow rate to tune the generation frequency and size of drops.
Calculate the mean drop volume using the aqueous flow rate divided by the drop generation frequency as measured by video capture.
Iteratively adjust both flow rates to achieve desired encapsulation rates and drop volumes.
Confirm stable ordered encapsulation.
Move the outlet tubing from the waste reservoir into a collection reservoir or feed it into another device for subsequent testing.
Determine the collection time based on the desired number of droplets and the calculated generation frequency.
Record the fraction of drops containing 0, 1, 2,..., N particles to quantify efficiency using either drop generation video results or by pipetting a sample of collected emulsion for inspection.
